newsitem.title: USA: U.S. pans Izetbegovic complaint on Dayton problems.
newsitem.headline: U.S. pans Izetbegovic complaint on Dayton problems.

text.p: The United States reacted scathingly on Thursday to a complaint by Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic that the Dayton peace accord was falling apart, calling it an unhelpful "litany of what has gone wrong."

Izetbegovic, Moslem chairman of Bosnia's collective presidency, handed Western envoys a nine-point document in Sarajevo on Monday alleging they were letting Serbs and Croats flout the accord, which created a two-part Bosnian state.

"The whole peace process in general has thus far had a negative direction which is leading to the further disintegration of Bosnia and Herzegovina," said the document, distributed by Bosnian embassies abroad.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns admitted there were "a lot of problems" but said: "It's not particularly helpful just to go out with a complete litany of what has gone wrong when a lot has gone right."

He said that following the 1995 U.S.-mediated Dayton pact, an international military force had kept the peace in Bosnia and there had also been national elections "which brought Mr Izetbegovic to the position where he is".
Economic aid had also begun to rebuild Sarajevo and other Bosnian cities, he told a news briefing.

"I don't think it's fair to disregard what has gone right, and to disregard the enormous effort that the Bosnian people have put into rebuilding their own country, and the enormous effort, frankly, that we've made," Burns said.

"We've got young men, American men and women, there who have put their lives on the line to safeguard the security of the Bosnian people. We've got aid workers there. And I'm not going to allow that to be dismissed by some statement."

Much of Izetbegovic's statement focused on attempts by Serbs to turn their half of Bosnia into a self-contained state instead of cooperating with the other half -- a Moslem-Croat federation -- in creating common Bosnian institutions.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Thursday pledged another $3.3 million to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to help it stage municipal elections in Bosnia in September.

Albright made the promise, which follows an earlier $5 million U.S. pledge, to former Italian Foreign Minister Susanna Agnelli who is trying to raise $50 million on behalf of the OSCE to hold the elections.
